drills.q: What is the unit memory moves in?
options: A cache line, 64 bytes on every x86-64 machine you will meet
A machine word, 8 bytes
A page, 4096 bytes
Whatever the load instruction asked for
drills.why: Read a single byte from a cold address and the hardware fetches all 64 containing it, evicting something else to make room. Whether the other 63 are useful is the whole game.

drills.q: How many cycles does a main memory fetch cost, roughly?
options: A couple of hundred
About ten
About twenty thousand
It depends entirely on the DRAM manufacturer
drills.why: Around eighty nanoseconds, which at a few gigahertz is a couple of hundred cycles of doing nothing. An L1 hit is about four.

options: Using the same address again soon
Using addresses in increasing order
Accessing memory at regular time intervals
Keeping a variable in a register across a loop
drills.why: Spatial locality is the other one: using an address near one you just used. Caches handle the first by keeping what was recently used and the second by fetching whole lines.

drills.q: Why is a linked list slow in a way an array is not?
options: Each node's address is known only after the previous one arrives, so the prefetcher cannot run ahead
Pointer dereferencing costs an extra instruction
Nodes are always allocated far apart
The nodes are larger than the values
drills.why: It is a fact about the prefetcher rather than about pointer arithmetic, and it is why the margins look implausible from the instruction counts alone.

drills.q: What does the prefetcher need before it can help?
options: A constant stride it can detect from the addresses touched
A hint instruction from the compiler
Sequential ascending addresses specifically
A loop the branch predictor has learned
drills.why: A loop walking an array in order rarely waits for memory at all, because the line arrived before it was asked for.

drills.q: Why is a stride of 4096 bytes pathological?
options: Every access lands in the same set, so only the ways in that one set are usable
It crosses a page boundary every time
It defeats the branch predictor
It exceeds the maximum prefetch distance
drills.why: A cache is not fully associative. Middle bits of the address choose a set, and a loop touching a few hundred kilobytes can behave as though the cache were 512 bytes.

drills.q: Why do numerical libraries pad row lengths?
options: To move the column stride off the period where every access collides
To keep rows aligned to page boundaries
To leave room for SIMD tails
To avoid false sharing between threads
drills.why: An array declared 1024 wide and allocated 1032 wide is not a mistake. The extra elements turn a loop that used one set back into one that uses the whole cache.

drills.q: Which miss is fixed by adding padding rather than by changing the algorithm?
options: A conflict miss
A capacity miss
A compulsory miss
All three
drills.why: Telling capacity from conflict is the difference between rewriting your algorithm and adding eight bytes to a struct.

options: The first touch of a line, which nothing avoids though prefetching can hide it
A miss caused by the cache being too small
A miss caused by two addresses mapping to the same set
A miss on a line another core invalidated
drills.why: Each of the three kinds has a different fix, which is why the classification earns its place.

drills.q: A loop reads one 8-byte field of every element in an array of 64-byte structs. What fraction of each fetched line is used?
options: One eighth
All of it, since the line is fetched once
One sixty-fourth
It depends on the prefetcher
drills.why: Splitting the fields into separate arrays lets the loop read only what it needs and use every byte of every line, which is routinely a factor of several.

drills.q: When does a structure of arrays make things worse?
options: When the code touches every field of one element
When the arrays exceed the cache size
When the fields have different sizes
It never does
drills.why: There is no correct layout, only a question about which access pattern is the hot one, and the transformation trades one for the other by the same factor.

drills.q: Why does loop order matter for a row-major array?
options: Walking by rows uses every byte of each line; walking by columns uses eight of each 64
Column order defeats the branch predictor
Row order allows vectorisation and column order does not
Column order crosses more page boundaries
drills.why: The loops compute identical results and differ in how many lines they ask for, which is a number you can count without running anything.

options: Two threads writing different variables on one line, invalidating each other's copy
Two threads reading the same variable without a lock
A cache line shared between two levels of the hierarchy
A stale copy left after a thread migrates cores
drills.why: Coherence is maintained per line rather than per byte, so two threads sharing no data behave as though they did. The fix is padding.

drills.q: What does blocking a computation change?
options: How many times each byte is fetched, from once per use to once per block
The total amount of arithmetic
The asymptotic complexity
The number of instructions executed
drills.why: Doubling the block size halves the traffic, until the block stops fitting in cache and the benefit disappears at once, which is why a tuned tile size is a measured constant.

drills.q: A profile shows low cache miss rates and poor performance. What should you do?
options: Look somewhere other than memory
Increase the block size
Add prefetch hints
Pad the data structures
drills.why: High misses at L1 and low at L3 means thrashing a small cache; high everywhere means the working set is genuinely large; low everywhere means the problem is elsewhere and another afternoon on memory is wasted.
